health-tech-leaders-and-designers-narrat.core: Posted in last 7 days Health Tech Leaders & Designers - Narrative Medicine Podcast What's the sentence in your own life you've never read closely enough? A few years ago, I sat in a room at Columbia with a sentence in front of me. Not a chart, not a deck, a sentence. The assignment was to read it as closely as I'd ever read anything. What is this story actually saying underneath what it says on the surface? That is Narrative Medicine, the discipline Dr. Rita Charon built to teach physicians how to hear a patient before they diagnose one truly. I came to it sideways, as an executive who'd spent a career launching products and revenue, and I left changed. Around the same time, I helped start a poetry salon at Grace Cathedral, Grace Poetry Sorts, where a room of strangers would sit with a poem that refused to resolve itself neatly. Neither experience had an obvious return on investment. Both rewired how I see a problem. I wanted that rigor of attention in how I lead and practice in my field of work. Not empathy as a soft skill bolted onto strategy, but empathy as the instrument that tells you which strategy is even worth building, whose voice is missing from the room, what the data isn't saying, where the frame is too narrow to see the whole picture. That shift, of widening the aperture before deciding what's in focus, made me a better human being long before it made me a better executive/leader. I'm honestly not sure those two things are separable. So today I'm sharing something I've been building quietly: Aperture: Widen the Frame, a podcast for people whose work sits at the collision of health, technology, and the human beings in the middle of both. Each episode brings together voices medicine alone doesn't usually put in the same room, with clinicians, scientists, poets, technologists, and designers, for conversations about what health and illness actually mean, not just how to build or sell around them. If you lead a team, sit on a board, or are trying to build the right thing in this space, my hope is you leave each episode with a sharper, fuller way of reading the people and problems in front of you, not just another data point. Episode 1, with Jane Sarasohn-Kahn, the renowned Health economist and Trend Weaver, is live now. https://lnkd.in/gg5ra_fM What's the sentence in your own life you've never read closely enough? uk-adults-80-lifetime-tech-economic-and-.core: Posted in last 7 days UK Adults 80+ - Lifetime Tech, Economic & Social Change Paid nonfiction book interview, £70/hour. Seeking someone aged 80+ in the UK to talk about a lifetime of technological, economic and social change Hi everyone! :) I am writing a nonfiction book and I am looking for one person aged 80+ in the UK who would be interested in taking part in a series of paid conversations over the next few weeks until September 28. The book is about the enormous technological, economic and social changes that can take place within a single lifetime. I am interested in changes such as postwar austerity and rising prosperity, changes in work and the economy, Thatcherism, changing relationships and family life, television and mass media, computers, the internet, smartphones and now AI. I am not looking for an expert or someone with an extraordinary CV. I am much more interested in finding someone who is curious, reflective and comfortable talking openly about how these changes shaped your life. The conversations could range naturally across childhood, work, money, relationships, family, technology, ageing, ambitions, disappointments, everyday routines and the ways Britain has changed around you. What interests me is the difference between how large historical or economic changes are described from the outside and what they actually feel like when they happen during one person's life. Time commitment: I would initially suggest around five hours of conversation, paid at £70 per hour, spread across several shorter interviews. If we both felt the conversations were working well, there could be further paid interviews afterwards. The interviews could initially take place by phone or video call, with the possibility of meeting in person depending on location. Anonymisation: You would appear under a pseudonym, with identifying details changed or removed, and we would agree clearly in writing beforehand how material from the conversations could be quoted, paraphrased or otherwise used. If you are interested, please send me a private message rather than posting personal information in the comments. It would be helpful to include your age, and a little about yourself. General questions are very welcome in the comments. And if this makes you think of a parent, grandparent, relative, neighbour or friend who might enjoy taking part, I would be very grateful if you passed this on to them. :)

cornell-ar-program-participants-ai-acade.core: Posted in last 7 days Cornell AR Program Participants - AI Academic Integrity Experiences Have you participated in the Accepting Responsibility program? A reporter wants to know Hi all. My name is Lee Gaines. I'm a reporter working on an assignment for the Hechinger Report about Cornell's response to academic integrity in the age of AI. I'm looking to talk to students who have participated in Cornell's "Accepting Responsibility" program. For anyone who hasn't heard of this, the AR program offers a workshop instead of the standard hearing and appeals process for some first-time academic integrity violations. Admins say that during the pilot phase of AR, more than half of the violations students got sent to the program for were AI-related. I'm interested in student perspectives; did the program help you handle academic challenges, clarify expectations around AI-use, and/or use AI in a way that doesn't undermine learning? Was it helpful or a waste of time? You don't need to comment here, or share anything sensitive under this post. You can DM me. Or email me: [email redacted]. We can discuss privacy and what you're comfortable sharing on the record before any interview. And I will only quote people with their explicit consent. And if you haven't participated in the AR program, I'm also intersted in hearing your general takes on Cornell's response to AI. Are professor policies on AI-use clear and/or fair? Have professors changed how they conduct exams? Anything else you think a reporter should know? Thanks! The Hechinger Report

independent-medicare-agents-plan-switchi.core: Posted in last 7 days Independent Medicare Agents - Plan Switching Before Open Enrollment Looking to narrow down what type of Insurance Agent or agency I need to locate. Can you help? Hey, I'll keep this quick and dirty. I'm just getting into a shadow of an idea that would make a good story about the insurance industry, specifically Medicare. I don't want to pursue someone who isn't involved in that type of Insurance sales so I figured I would ask here. How would I label, locate or identify an agency that handles Medicare Renewals? For example, say you're 74, retired, and someone calls to get you to switch over your Aetna to Humana, or your Devoted coverage to Alignment and then to United Health Care. I'm curious as to how this can happen before open enrollment, or being on the do not call registry, or with the blessing of the regulators. Just seems difficult to change over someone that often. Are there commissions? Promotions? Is it worth it as a livelihood? I looked at the NPN on a sample Application and it's for an agent in Texas. I went down a hole and only found a name, independent, but is active with numerous companies, no phone number besides the direct line to UH. Also it seems the agent is actually located in Zimbabwe. I'd really like to know more about this method of sales, the legalities, the loopholes, etc if anyone would like to speak on it. I would like to know all that I can and figured there would be some insight on this subreddit. If you don't feel comfortable saying anything in public, you can pm. Thank you to whomever can respond.
